source.title: Rethinking ResNets: improved stacking strategies with high-order schemes for image classification
source.authors: Zhengbo Luo; Zitang Sun; Wei-Lian Zhou; Zizhang Wu; S. Kamata

record.tranche_reason: Compares training accuracy and loss across residual-network stacking strategies on CIFAR-10, but does not test memorization of random or corrupted labels or whether training error reaches zero.
record.gate_note: Figure 12 is described as reporting ResNet-58 training accuracy and loss. The text says higher-order stacking improves on the baseline, but gives no training-accuracy values; results cited from other papers are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study uses residual shortcuts, He initialization and batch normalization to evaluate its own stacking strategies. Its reported training comparisons do not establish near-zero training error, and its other experiments do not isolate any claim version's specified mechanism or comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that higher-order stacking improves performance, convergence and robustness, and delays rather than eliminates degradation. Their degradation discussion should not be read as a demonstrated increase in training error.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD and He initialization with batch normalization to compare higher-order residual-block stacking on CIFAR-10; it does not reproduce the random-label memorization experiments in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: Stacking scheme and network depth; the authors report that higher-order schemes have increasingly evident advantages in deeper cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher-order stacking improves the qualitative training-accuracy and loss curves for ResNet-58. Table 4 reports speedups over Euler stacking to 80%/85% training accuracy: midpoint 2.27/2.28, RK4 4.43/3.92, fixed RK8 3.31/3.53 and adaptive RK8 3.84/3.03.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-order residual stacking accelerates reaching intermediate training-accuracy targets on CIFAR-10 under the tested recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 9 states that ResNet-86 with Euler stacking diverges at learning rates of 0.13 and above, while midpoint converges near 0.2, RK4 at 0.23 and Verner RK8 at 0.4 or above.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-order residual stacking increases learning-rate tolerance in the tested CIFAR-10 setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 3 reports depth-dependent test-accuracy differences among residual stacking schemes; the authors interpret these as delayed but eventual degradation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual stacking strategy affects how CIFAR-10 test accuracy changes with network depth.

record.problems: The relevant training-accuracy results are presented in Figure 12 without numeric values in the text. The text does not establish near-zero training error or test random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the text describes the training-accuracy and loss comparison only qualitatively, and the figure-only values cannot be extracted from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Whether final training classification error reaches zero or near zero. Figure 12's final values are unavailable in the supplied text; times to 80% and 85% training accuracy do not establish this. CIFAR-100 and corrupted or random labels are not tested.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima and extra student neurons.

Training-error degradation across depths in plain networks versus networks with identity shortcuts. The reported depth comparisons concern residual architectures and test accuracy; the degradation discussion does not establish higher training error.
Effects of alternative initializations on training speed, signal propagation or trainable depth. Initialization is held fixed while stacking changes.

Recovery above the initial linearized stability threshold, transient loss increases with curvature drops, and full-batch edge-of-stability dynamics. The learning-rate sweep measures convergence or divergence without these diagnostics.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including a Fixup comparison. Batch normalization is used throughout.

record.verdict_notes: There are no extracted rows to fix. The omitted Figure 12 results are declared in rows_left_out. Test accuracies in Tables 3 and 4 cannot establish V1's training-error claim or V3's training degradation claim.

versions.untested_parts: The text reports training-accuracy comparisons on CIFAR-10, but does not state whether training classification error reaches zero or near zero, or test corrupted or random labels, smaller models, early stopping, or regularized recipes.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
